walkthroughs.body_html:
Hazardous Environments — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Hazardous Environments brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Hazardous Environments.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

options: Sahel
Maghreb
Cape
Horn of Africa

mcqs.q: What is the maximum rainfall in hot deserts?
options: 100mm
250mm
500mm

mcqs.q: How do rivers transport their load?
options: By traction (rolling large stones along the bed), saltation (bouncing smaller pebbles), suspension (carrying fine sediment in the flow) and solution (dissolved minerals).
Because LICs have better infrastructure than HICs.
Rivers transport everything by pushing it along the bottom.
Rivers can only transport material when they are in flood.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a choropleth and an isoline map?
options: Choropleth maps are for showing churches and isoline maps are for showing roads.
Choropleth and isoline maps are the same thing.
Choropleths use coloured/shaded areas to show data values per region (e.g. population density by county); isoline maps use lines connecting points of equal value (e.g. contours, isobars).
Rivers can only transport material when they are in flood.
